It was after the edited photos went round in Class 9. I stopped answering in class, even when I knew the answer. I ate lunch in the library, alone. At night I lay awake replaying every laugh.

The worst part wasn't the photos. It was being sure nobody would believe me, or that telling would just make it bigger.

One night Ankita came into my room, sat on the floor and said, "I saw the photos. I'm not leaving till you talk." I cried for the first time in weeks. She woke our parents that same night, and Papa sat with us until two, promising we'd go to the principal together in the morning. We did.

Class teacher's note, Thursday

Saurabh used to be one of the first to answer in physics. For three weeks he has not spoken in class. He eats his lunch alone on the back stairs and looks exhausted; he told me he "just isn't sleeping well."

When I asked if something was wrong, he said, "I'm fine, Ma'am." His hands were shaking.

Today Minakshi from his class stayed back and quietly showed me messages from a group chat mocking Saurabh. She said he had stopped replying to everyone, even her.

I found Saurabh at the back stairs at lunch and sat with him. I told him I had seen the messages, that it was not his fault, and that I believed him before he said anything. He cried. I took him to the counsellor, informed the principal, and phoned his father before the end of school.

— Minakshi's class teacher, Mrs Das

qa.q: Where did Saurabh eat his lunch?
qa.a: Alone on the back stairs.

qa.q: What does Saurabh saying "I'm fine" with shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is not fine; he feels hurt, lonely and afraid, perhaps sure no one would believe or help.

qa.q: What did Mrs Das do well?
qa.a: She took Minakshi's evidence seriously, sat with Saurabh, said she believed him and it wasn't his fault, and got the counsellor, principal and his father involved the same day.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt showing the messages to the teacher?
qa.a: She was probably nervous but relieved, worried for Saurabh after he stopped replying even to her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Saurabh withdrawing, eating alone and saying he is fine, and the teacher acting the same day after a classmate shares evidence.

Sunday night

Didn't go down for dinner again. Told Ma I had a headache.

A month since Tushar's group made that page about me. I don't talk in class anymore. If I say anything, someone laughs. I eat my tiffin in the chemistry lab where nobody goes.

I can't sleep. I keep checking the page at 2 a.m. to see what they've added.

Ma keeps asking if I'm okay. I keep saying yes. What's the point? If I tell her, she'll go to school, and they'll just say it's a joke, and then it'll be worse. Nobody would believe how bad it is anyway.

Later —

Ma came up with a plate and saw my screen before I could close it. She sat on my bed, read everything, and held my hand. She said, "I believe you. This is not your fault." She called Papa home and they rang my class teacher tonight. Tomorrow we go in together.

You asked what it's like to be in the middle? I'm Aadhya. I'll tell you honestly.

There's a girl in our class, Uma. Some girls started a meme page about her clothes. The first time I saw it, I laughed. It was a reflex. Then I saw Uma's face across the room, and I felt awful.

After that, every time the group posted, my stomach knotted. I wanted to say "stop." But I've seen what happens to girls who go against them. They'd find something about me by lunch.

So I did smaller things. I didn't like the posts. I didn't forward them. One night I messaged Uma privately: "That page is horrible. You don't deserve it." She replied, "Thanks. I thought everyone agreed with it."

That line stayed with me. She thought everyone agreed. My one message told her not everyone did. The next morning I showed our class teacher the page, quietly, after assembly.

Uday, you did right to tell me about those messages. Now let your Darshan chacha tell you something from when I was in Class 11.

A group of boys kept sending me cruel messages every night. I was ashamed. I thought telling would make me look weak. I deleted everything so nobody would see.

That was the turning point: saving the proof and telling someone who took it seriously.

Vaibhav's phone was at four percent, the board exam was in two days, and the messages wouldn't stop. A fake account had been posting edited photos of him all evening.

He wanted to delete everything and throw the phone in a drawer.

His friend Sarika, video-calling from her own room, said, "Don't delete anything. Screenshot. Now, before your phone dies."

He did, fast: eleven screenshots. Then he plugged in and she made him email them to himself, and to her.

"Now tell your mother," Sarika said. "Tonight."

"She's stressed about my exam. I don't want to make it worse."

"This is making it worse. Telling isn't weak, Vaibhav. It's how you protect yourself."

He went downstairs. His mother read every screenshot. She said, "Thank you for showing me," and emailed his class teacher that night. The next morning the school reported the account and called in the students involved, without moving Vaibhav's exam seat.

Santosh sat at the dining table in their Nagpur flat and slid his phone across to his father, Harish.

"I saved them," he said. "Screenshots. From the group. For three weeks."

Harish scrolled. His face tightened. There were photos of Santosh with insults typed over them, and voice notes mocking him.

"Why didn't you tell me earlier?"

"I thought you'd say I was weak. Or that I should hit back."

Harish put the phone down. "Telling me is not weak. It's the smart thing. Thank you."

The next morning Harish went with Santosh to meet the principal and showed her everything. She listened, kept copies, and called in the students' parents that week. When one teacher suggested moving Santosh to another section "to avoid trouble," the principal said no: "He did nothing wrong. They're the ones who'll change."

The meeting in the counsellor's room at the Lucknow school lasted an hour. Jasleen sat on one side, arms crossed. Salma sat on the other, next to her mother.

Jasleen had already been suspended for a week for the posts she made about Salma. Today was the other part.

The counsellor asked Jasleen to read aloud three of her own posts. Halfway through the second one, Jasleen's voice cracked. "I didn't think... it looks different read out loud."

Salma said quietly, "I stopped going to dance class because of these."

Jasleen looked at her for the first time. "I'm sorry. I did it because the group laughed. I wanted them to like me." The counsellor arranged weekly sessions for Jasleen to talk about that.

Two weeks later, Salma went back to dance class. Her friends went with her. And in the class chat, when someone started a new joke about another girl, three people typed, "Not again. Stop."

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when she read her posts aloud?
qa.a: Her voice cracked; she felt ashamed, realising how cruel the posts looked read out loud.

qa.q: How did this process help both girls and the class?
qa.a: Jasleen faced consequences, understood the harm and got counselling for her need for approval; Salma got support to return to dance; the class learned to speak up instead of staying silent.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing Jasleen's apology?
qa.a: She may feel some relief and a little more confident, seeing Jasleen understand the harm.

grounding: After consequences, Jasleen faces the harm of her posts in a counselling meeting and gets support, while Salma regains confidence and the class learns silence has a cost.

I was one of the people who watched Lokesh bully Anish for most of Class 10 and said nothing. I'm Manjula, and this is how it ended.
